None of these workers can leave the Sudbury basin and pick up a job in southern Ontario. That is a dangerous situation. We have not developed the mining industry in this country to maturity. We do not have the infrastructure to develop the resource to a finished product. That is where the jobs are. They are in finishing the raw resource, not shipping it out.
Export Development Act
Every time the Export Development Corporation makes a loan to a multinational mining company for it to develop its resource abroad, it does us considerable harm down the road. That is compounded by the announcement in the budget speech that the mining companies will now get a 100 per cent write-off on the development of new mines. Those policies are superimposed on a situation where we have developed over the years and will continue to develop as hewers of wood and drawers of water. I cannot see any attempt to turn that around. It would be better, as recommended in the booklet of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, to go from mining to manufacturing. It is a chain. It is interconnected.
Recognizing that, would it not have been logical for the Minister of Finance to have given the 100 per cent write-off on developing the infrastructure at the source where the resource is mined to take it to a finished product? Would that not have made more sense? It would have at least indicated that we are trying to break out of this vicious cycle of ripping out stuff and shipping it abroad. We cannot go on in that way.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) comes up with doling out more Canada Works money. Does that make sense, shoving it one end and allowing a rip-off program at the other?
How do you justify the Department of Economic Expansion, which has designated areas, pumping out money to industry to go into those areas, while at the same time the Export Development Corporation is inciting corporations to stay and in fact expand in the golden triangle? If you look at those new programs, you see that one negates the other. It does not make any sense.
I now want to touch on the Panamanian deal. That is quite an interesting situation. It is a real rat's nest. There we have one of the world's largest copper deposits.
Let us look at the firms that have been involved there. Canadian Javelin first opened the project. John Doyle was the promoter of the Canadian Javelin Company. Later on Noran-da became involved. Note all these good corporate patriotic citizens. Guess who finally ended up managing the whole shebang? Guess who is doing that while enjoying a nice 20 per cent equity in the project? It is none other than Texas Gulf Incorporated. What is a nice Canadian Development Corporation Company like that doing in such a den of snakes? Canadian taxpayers own that company through the Canadian Development Corporation. One would expect that corporation to be dedicated to creating jobs in Canada. I do not understand it.
The minister says that operation will go into effect in 1983. It will compete in the area of jobs with the Canadian copper industry which does not have the infrastructure strength that it ought to have at this time.
I see, Mr. Speaker, you are giving me the signal like horses coming through the gate for the start. I will, therefore, conclude. The argument we make is that the mining sector should be excluded from the provinces of the Export Development Corporation. Jobs are at issue. An infrastructure around the

November 28, 1978
Export Development Act
mining sector in this country is important. If the EDC has money to lend, it ought to be loaned for the development of that sort of infrastructure and to develop those kinds of jobs in Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: AMENDING MEASURE TO EXCLUDE MINING CORPORATIONS FROM APPLICATION OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Export Development Act voted in 1969 gave extensive powers to the corporation, which was in a position to borrow, deal with or provide security for loans, conclude insurance contracts, grant export credits and provide guarantees for export and investment operations abroad. I think that the best way to proceed is to analyze its activities and their effects in each sector.
Let us begin by the export loans area. Those loans are granted to importing countries to enable them to purchase goods and services from a Canadian supplier. It makes it possible to preserve if not to create some jobs. In 1977, the value of export financing exceeded $1 billion for the first time. This was an increase of 30 per cent over the 1976 figure which amounted to $736 million. Canadian export sales made possible by those loans were beneficial to more than 50 exporters and over 250 main subcontractors under 42 agreements signed with 22 countries. That money is not going out of the country, it is used to pay for the purchase of machinery manufactured in Canada which will serve in the development of these projects. As far as the export credit insurance program is concerned, this service offers to Canadian export companies general or individual insurance policies which cover any risk which commercial insurance companies do not cover. Among these risks, let us mention wars that might start in the importer's country, default in payment by the foreign purchaser of Canadian services and products, and so on.
These insurance policies favour the export of Canadian goods and eliminates certain risks which unfortunately do exist in some countries. Mr. Speaker, in 1977 the balance of insured exports reached the record level of $1.45 billion. The increase in the value of exports insured in 1976 is about $100 million. Moreover, the corporation offers services to companies wishing to invest in foreign countries, which allows Canadian businessmen to invest without worrying about policies which could jeopardize their investments.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like to call the attention of the House to the fact that the corporation is relying more and more on international money markets as a source of funds. Which means that it is borrowing abroad to lend abroad. The result of this, as far as Our balance of payment is concerned, is to transform a credit operation into a cash operation. Thanks to this new procedure, the corporation need no longer borrow from the consolidated revenue fund, as it used to.
I should like to remind hon. members that this Crown corporation is a profitable venture, as its net benefits for 1977

amounted to $18.7 million, an increase of 6 per cent over 1976. Our per capita exports amount to $2,000 and represent approximately 22 per cent. Canada ranks among the top countries of the world which rely most on their exports. In 1976 it could become the seventh largest exporting country of the world for the value of its exports and the second for its per capita value.
This clearly demonstrates the importance of our exports and of the part the Export Development Corporation must continue to play to help our country create new jobs and realize its trading potential.
We must rely more and more on the export of goods and related services to ensure our economic growth and reinforce our industrial sector. I have often heard hon. members say in the House that our manufacturing industries could not sustain competition or that our deficit was way too big in view of the products manufactured here. Surely, the Export Development Corporation has helped enormously to increase the exportation of our manufactured products.
The EDC is probably the most misunderstood corporation in Canada. Many members opposite and many Canadians do not really understand the government and the EDC role. A few months ago there were lay-offs at Inco. Deep concern was expressed because Inco had built nickel mines in Guatemala and Indonesia and it was said that in some way this resulted in fewer jobs for Canadians. In this particular case, EDC granted approximately $20.75 million for the Guatemala mine and $57.25 million for the Indonesia mine.
I will explain what really happened. The project was well underway and Inco came to EDC to obtain financing guarantees. It stated it would buy about $1 million's worth of goods in Canada. EDC accepted that amount as being sufficient and, after many discussions, finally obtained that the other party agree to purchase more goods manufactured in Canada, in fact up to $60 million worth of them. About $900 million were spent on the project and nickel mines were opened up in both countries thanks to financing advanced by Japan, Germany and Great Britain. On the other hand, EDC gave assistance by selling mining equipment in both countries. We sold for 4,800 man-years of work in Canada, which is why I can say that EDC thus creates jobs.
Here is another example of the work performed by the Export Development Corporation, with a view of creating jobs in Canada: On April 5 last, the biggest insurance contract ever for a company, covering sales for $1 billion, was signed by Bell Canada with Saudi Arabia; that figure includes $250 million in guarantees and $180 million in export credit guarantees. That sale will represent no less than 2,500 man-years of employment for Canadians. I am giving you those few specific examples to give parliament and our fellow citizens an idea of what EDC really accomplishes.
On March 9, 1978 it agreed to make loans for a total amount of $57 million towards the sale to Argentina of
November 28, 1978

technical and mining equipment estimated at $67 million made by the Canadian companies Sandwell and Company Limited of Vancouver, and SNC-Rust Limited of Montreal. There again, those decisions led to the creation of an incredible number of jobs in Canada. On October 3, 1978, EDC announced that it had agreed to lend $218 million to H.A. Simons (Overseas) Ltd. of Vancouver, to help it build a pulp mill in Czechoslovakia. The following day, Mr. Speaker, it announced that it had set up an important line of credit, for $1.2 billion, with Algeria, which will allow the creation or continuation of Canadian jobs, for Canadians, in the country. Small business profit as much by these operations as large ones. For example, one need only refer to the list of subcontractors for the steel mill project on the Raritan River, in Perth Amboy, New Jersey.
Suppliers include Provincial Crane Limited of Niagara Falls, which will supply $2.6 million worth of cranes; the Lake Ontario Steel Company of Whitby which will supply $461,000 worth of steel reinforcements; Canadian General Electric of Scarborough which will supply $1,780,000 worth of main control continuous current motors and thus create 77 man-years of work; Whiting Equipment Ltd. of Welland will supply a $1,521,000 electric arc kiln; Concast Canada Limited of Montreal will supply a $2,230,000 molding machine and Brown Boveri Canada Limited of Pointe-Claire will supply $1,730,000 of electric systems and controls and thus create 54 man-years of work.
Here are other companies who took part in similar operations.
The EDC helped Versatile Manufacturing Limited of Winnipeg, shipyards both on the east and west coasts, and mining and nickel industries in Ontario. In fact, it helped substantially the nickel industry. If we are to encourage our secondary industries, we need agencies like the EDC. All the large exporting countries have exactly the same type of agency. Anyone who has the slightest idea of what economics are all about knows that it is ridiculous to question that corporation, perhaps to ask for its abolition, to refuse to export machinery and equipment to countries like Poland.
We would not leave our industries to their own fate on world markets where they will have to face the American EX-IM or Japanese, German and French financial companies; they need the help of a similar agency. The EDC works hard to help Canadian manufacturers, just like EX-IM helps U.S. manufacturers and financial companies help Japanese, German and French manufacturers.
The main criticism levelled at the Export Development Corporation concerns the fact that it is used to finance industries which compete with those already established in Canada. Since certain people and certain parties have left Canadians with the false impression that by financing Canadian industries in other countries, the EDC somehow contributes to the loss of jobs in Canada, I believe it is important to refute this
Export Development Act
immediately in the House. Major capital projects will be implemented in Indonesia, Poland and Iran whatever happens, with or without Canada's participation.
These projects will be launched. Third world countries and other developing countries will build their own paper plants. If they have nickel or copper deposits, they will not be content to do nothing about them.
If my friends in the opposition do not agree with me on this point, if they refuse to admit that these projects will be seen through with or without our participation, if they wish Japanese, West German or British companies to become established throughout the world while ours remain in Canada, let them say so! Let the Japanese, the West Germans and the British open up mines in Indonesia and Guatemala. Let them submerge us with their capital while we do nothing and refuse to invest in industries which could compete with our own. When they suggest that capital projects in Poland, Iran and Indonesia would not be carried out without the participation of Canada, they are misleading Canadians. These projects will become reality whatever happens. The only issue is whether Canadian manufacturers will benefit from a part of these projects. It is only a matter of allowing them to participate.
There is no alternative. We must simply decide whether Canada will participate in certain projects and whether employment will be created because of this participation. It is ridiculous to pretend that these financing programs reduce the number of jobs in Canada. This may create a certain competition for Canadian products, but if Canada did not participate in these projects, this competition would come from Japan, Germany or the United Kingdom. Their plants manufacture the material. You either take advantage of it or think we are poor economists. In this era of instantaneous world communications, locally minded people do not go very far. Indeed, the figures speak for themselves. The Export Development Corporation is a Crown corporation of which Canadians can be proud. The good reputation it has all around the world is shared by Canada and all its people. In addition, through its operations it contributes a lot to the industrial and economic expansion of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to add a few comments in the debate on Bill C-205 proposed by my friend, the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez). The hon. member seems to have a one-track mind: right train, wrong track. Or to put it a little more diplomatically, he has a single-minded approach to the subject of the Export Development Corporation. The questions he has raised here today are not new. He raised them during the debates on Bill C-47 in May and June of 1977 and on Bill C-36 in April, May and June, 1978. I will elaborate on that point in a few minutes. On the other hand, one thing I would like to know is how the hon. member and his colleagues in the New Democratic Party, with its humanitarian posture, feel about development and jobs in less privileged countries than Canada including-and I say this respectfully-his own place of origin, Guyana.
Let us look at what the Export Development Corporation does. It is probably the most written about and talked about Crown corporation-favourably-and probably one of the least understood. First, let me describe what it does not do. It never gives away money, never subsidizes anyone for any reason, never lends money to Canadian companies, is selffinancing and is not in the aid business.
According to EDC brochures, its goal is to facilitate Canadian export trade through the provision of loans, insurance and foreign investment guarantees. Its insurance covers many risks. It can be protection against non-payment for

goods and services by foreign buyers, covering either commercial risks, bankruptcy, insolvency, repudiation of debt and so forth or political risks, war, riot, insurrection, convertibility problems and other problems. This insurance can be on all export volume in a year or on a contract by contract basis. The EDC also provides surety insurance to Canadian exporters, covering the risk of wrongful call on bank guarantees or surety bonds by foreign buyers. A new service offered is contractors' surety, which covers contractors involved in construction projects abroad. The EDC's insurance covers all sizes and varieties of exporters, large and small.
' Another service is foreign investment guarantees. This insurance covers investments abroad by Canadian companies. Insurance is offered only when the EDC is convinced that the proposed investment is beneficial and acceptable to the host country and, more importantly, that there is a major return to the Canadian economy.
The service which attracts most of the attention and misguided criticism is the EDC's loan facility. The EDC lends money to foreign buyers of Canadian goods and services. These loans are fully secured and negotiated at rates of interest above the cost of money to the EDC.
Funds for these loans come from world capital markets, not out of taxpayers' pockets. The money never leaves Canada, as the EDC, acting on behalf of the foreign buyer, disburses directly to the Canadian exporter as he exports. To assure that Canadian jobs are being created or maintained, the EDC ensures that in each transaction Canadian content is maximized. In recognition of the importance of the role of developing and maximizing Canadian industry participation in each transaction, the EDC closely monitors the application of corporate Canadian content objectives. Thus, when loans are made to finance sales of Canadian equipment and services to projects being built in other countries, jobs in Canada's manufacturing industry are being created or maintained. One thing must remain clear: If there are no Canadian sales, then there is no EDC financing or any EDC insurance.
All the major trading nations of the world provide government support to facilitate trade. EDC facilities help Canadian exporters to meet competition on a non-subsidized basis. If a product or service is competitive in price, quality, delivery and service, the EDC enables the exporter to offer competitive credit terms. The EDC attempts to neutralize financing as a consideration in the awarding of contracts.
This bill is based on one of the most frequent misconceptions about the EDC. The hon. member feels that the EDC and Canada should not finance sales to industries or projects which may prove competitive to the Canadian mining industry. This rests on the belief that such action would benefit Canada by eliminating this competition. The problem with that thesis is that, by corollary, it must presume that Canada can prevent another country from developing projects and, that Canada is the sole proprietor of viable technology. However, the fact remains that, whether we like it or not, we live in a fiercely competitive world economic environment. If Canada does not sell mining technology, Great Britain, France, Germany,

Mr. Speaker, as I rise to take part in this debate on Bill C-2 regarding the Health Resources Fund Act it is interesting to note that I was here in the House when the original bill was first introduced by the present government House leader, who was then health minister. I have followed the act's progress with a good deal of feeling over the years because of my interest in how it might increase research activity, an increase that was certainly necessary at the time. This is apparent when we stop to consider that more scientists lived and worked in this century than lived and worked since dawn. When we realize this we must concede that there have been terrific advances in science, not only because of the numbers involved, but because each discovery has led to something else and there has been a compounding effect. Scientists have carried on with new ideas and new discoveries.
I have listened to the speeches during this debate with a great deal of satisfaction. They have been excellent speeches. I

November 28, 1978
Health Resources Fund Act
was in the House when national medicare and the Health Resources Fund Act were introduced. Let me give a little of the scientific history of the nineteenth century. During that time Jenner discovered vaccination which has proved to be such a boon. This was a scientific discovery by a general practitioner in the U.K. In France there was the discovery by Pasteur of the germ theory, and Lister put this theory into practice in surgery using an antiseptic spray in the operating room to kill bacteria. I have had the privilege of seeing the equipment used in the operating rooms of hospitals in England, here in Canada and elsewhere. In addition, Madame Curie in France made a great discovery-radium.
At the beginning of the twentieth century our average life expectancy was a little over 40 years. Today the average life expectancy is about 75 years. In the early days infectious diseases were our main killers. We had our pneumonias, scarlet fever, typhoid fever and diphtheria. These were the major killers of individuals up to age 35.
This picture has almost changed completely. The big killer today of individuals from birth to age 35 is accident. This is an altogether different world from that point of view, and an altogether different world we are living in from a scientific point of view.
At the beginning of this century the wards of the existing hospitals were filled to overflowing with patients suffering from typhoid fever in the fall months. Every bed in the hospitals was filled, and you could see the ice buckets out in the wards for the fever baths. I have talked to doctors who have experienced this. We then learned that this was a disease caused by the environment and hygiene. We then took measures to stamp out typhoid fever by isolating the organism and developing a vaccine, thus treating the environment. Had this not been done the first world war could not have been fought on the scale it was.
From there we go on to the antitoxins and the development of toxoids to prevent diphtheria. I can still remember vividly an experience, when I was seven years of age living on the farm, concerning the family next door. The mother had gone to Toronto where she had died in hospital. One of her children who had been to Toronto contracted diphtheria, and in that family of 13 five of the children were wiped out in the space of about three weeks. Diphtheria antitoxins did not come into general use until around 1905, and they were used on this particular family.
After the antitoxins we go on to the great discovery by Banting and Best that wrote history for Canada around the world. They had discovered a treatment for diabetes. I was raised not far from the town where Dr. Banting was born, and I can remember his telling me about the impression that he had when he was a young school boy of seeing a young girl in his class who had diabetes. Day after day he watched her get thinner and thinner, and every time she went by the water pump she had to take a drink. She eventually died. There was always the strange smell on her, which we now recognize as

acetone. That gave Banting an impression which carried him through medical school until he and Dr. Best did research on the pancreas of dogs at the University of Toronto and finally found a treatment for diabetes.
Insulin allows the diabetic to live a normal life, contributing greatly not only to the economics of this land but to the health and well being of people. One of the outstanding doctors of diabetes in the city of Toronto was a diabetic himself who lived and was able to practice as a doctor because of the discovery of insulin.
Another great story is the one of two scientists, Minot and Murphy, at the University of Chicago who discovered that an extract of liver would cure pernicious anemia. There probably is not a confrere of mine in this House that has ever seen a case of pernicious anemia where a person would have a relapse of fever and the red blood cell count would go down. It is similar to a cancer of the blood. These two researchers found that a shot of extract from the liver every week would cure and control this disease. We no longer see the disease any more than we see a case of diabetes which is not properly treated.
Sulfa was the first drug to be discovered that was able to kill bacteria. In 1936 I brought some prontosil home from the Mayo Clinic where they had been using it to cure strep infections, the scarlet fevers, tonsillitis and diseases such as that. Patients responded very well to this treatment and it took strep out of the category of a dangerous disease.
The next drug used was dagenan. I spoke to a lady on Sunday whom I had once treated for pneumonia by the use of dagenan. After dagenan came the discovery of the penicillins. A researcher found that bacteria would not grow on a mould, and from that mould came penicillin. This drug has saved so many young people's lives, particularly those who had pneumonia. The death rate from pneumonia, before the discovery of penicillin was one in five, but today it is about one in 25, and that rate will be cut down further with the development of the newer, stronger penicillins. The next drugs to be developed were the aureomycins and the tetracyclines and so forth, again setting a new pattern for killing off infections.
At the end of this era we found that the whole ball game had changed and that we now had to face the fact that we were running into chronic diseases. We found that one in every ten people had a cardiovascular disease of some type by the age of 50. After this came the arthritic disorders, diseases of the respiratory system, emphysema, etc. These are chronic diseases and by the time people had reached the age of 60 they had four times the illness they had at 30 years of age. This brought to the fore the need for chronic care and the problem of research, because at this point we were treating chronic diseases, not the acute infections of previous days.
What has happened in the meantime? We have gone through the fifties and the sixties and we find that four million people have immigrated into this country in a few years. We are short of doctors because very few of the medical schools have enlarged sufficiently to meet this increase in population. What we were doing then was cheating, because it now costs more than $100,000 to put a person through medical school, as
November 28, 1978

compared with $60,000 then. A third or half of the people entering the field of medicine were either graduates or immigrants who came to this country from some other country in which they had been educated.
We talk about foreign aid. If that is not taking foreign aid from countries that could ill afford it, I do not know what it is. Most of these countries had a doctor-patient ratio which was much higher than Canada's. In India there is probably one doctor for every 5,000 people, whereas in Canada it would be about one doctor for every 2,000 people.
Something had to be done, and as a result the Hall commission report came about. This House approved the establishment of the Hall commission to determine what could be done about the enlargement of medical schools, among other things. They realized that they were getting into a chronic care situation and that more research would be needed. The report of the Hall commission was largely adopted.
In 1966 the Health Resources Fund Act was passed on the basis that it would add facilities to medical schools to give them an opportunity to bring in teachers, professors and scientists to develop the best medical schools in the world. The principle behind it was to give us the best there was, and they pledged $500 million for a period of 15 years, which would bring us to 1981. In 1978 we find that we have been cut off.
I believe I forgot to mention the disease poliomyelitis when I mentioned the great work that has been done by scientists on the North American continent and around the world. But when they found a preventive measure for this crippling disease which could kill a young person in the space of 48 hours, and if it did not kill it could cripple and handicap a person for life, the return on polio research amounted to more than $2,000 for every $1 spent, although it is almost impossible to arrive at any kind of an accurate figure. Nothing pays off so well as research.
Here we have a government that brought in a health resources act now wanting to cut off the money supply. It seems incredible, when one looks at the Auditor General's report and finds such carelessness in the spending of money, that this government dares to cut off something that saves people's lives. There are so many crippling diseases. The statistics show that cancer kills one person in every four. Emphysema is on the increase. There are many other diseases from which people suffer. There is hardly a family in Canada that will not be touched somewhere along the line by a disease that we have yet to conquer. We can only conquer these diseases by continued research.
At this point I would like to pay tribute to those researchers who spend their lives doing this type of work, many of whom at the end of their careers have discovered nothing but have steadfastly worked hard in the hope that some miraculous breakthrough will occur. These researchers suffer trials, tribulations and frustrations in an endeavour to restore health to the people of this country and throughout the world. Many of them have given their lives by experimenting with injections or
Health Resources Fund Act
treatments performed on themselves. I say with a source of pride that there are still people who are willing to enter this field of endeavour without adequate funds or any kind of tribute.
A cramping of resources in the health care field has occurred over the last ten years. It has been a fight all the way to get a little more money for the research necessary. At the beginning of this century there were few scientists. Today we have many. We have conquered many diseases but there are still chronic diseases to deal with.
If we look at the statistics we find that there are more than two million people over the age of 65. There are diseases of all kinds that can take a man who is at the height of his career and in the prime of his life out of the work force and make him a liability. It is our responsibility to see that we retain the health and work abilities of those people as long as it is possible to do so, and in many cases beyond the age of 60 and 65. As hon. members know, a bill was introduced in the United States stating that it will not be mandatory to retire at the age of 65 if a person is physically and mentally fit. Instead a person will be allowed to carry on working until the age of 70. If there is enough money put into research to keep people healthy, perhaps people will be able to work until they are 75. If that cannot be accomplished the social service scheme will be in trouble.
There is another bill in the United States covering people academically trained. If they are physically and mentally well they can carry on without time limitation. This not only applies to the field of health resources but also industry. The government admits they should be spending five times as much, and yet here we are cutting funds. Can you tell me, Mr. Speaker, what is wrong with a government that does that?
The other night I went outside the House of Commons at about eleven o'clock. I looked across the river and saw that every one of those buildings on the other side was lit up. 1 thought of people raising families. With the rate of inflation today many families are finding it difficult to pay their electric light and heating bills. I could take you to homes owned by old people and pensioners who are paying their taxes, heating and lighting, but the government does not subsidize them as far as housing is concerned. These senior citizens have been neglected. There is, however, subsidized housing in some cities. When I looked across at all these buildings lit up it occurred to me that for the cost of one night's electricity for those buildings something more beneficial could be done. Not only that, I thought of the cost of construction of those buildings. There is no return on that and no research from a project such as that. Space that is empty is being paid for in Ottawa. The provinces are already saying that they are not getting enough money for things they want to do.
There is something wrong. I do not believe the government realize what they are doing. I do not believe this government understand what research is. I do not believe they understand that they have cut off research or that there will be a breakdown in the social system. The minister is a nice lady but I do not know if she is tough enough in cabinet to tell her col-

November 28, 1978
Health Resources Fund Act
leagues what the situation is. Once the government starts on a path of cutting funds for research, researchers will be lost. They will leave one by one. Good teachers will be lost. Many universities have lost professors over the last two years that now have leading positions in the United States. Once these people have left and are set up in another university it is very difficult to entice them back. Every day we lose some people in this field. We are losing younger people as well, because these people say that research has been cut back 20 per cent, and that means that 20 per cent of the jobs will disappear.
This is not only a disastrous course in the economic field, but a disastrous course pure and simple when it comes down to the saving of lives and doing the necessary research. 1 hope the government will take another look at this, but not in three or five years because by then we will have lost our researchers. We are losing them and our economic value.
1 hope the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) will realize you cannot hurt the people of this country from the standpoint of not providing the funds to find a cure for cancer and disabling disease. We must find a way to treat people beyond the age of 60 or 65 so that our whole social system does not break down.
In conclusion, I hope the Prime Minister will take another look at this before allowing it to go completely by the board.

speakeroldname: Miss Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in taking part in this debate, it is a very welcome privilege to follow the eloquent plea made by my colleague from Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard) to the government benches. He asked the government to realize its responsibility, and to take it seriously, with regard to the development of innovative research in this country and the stimulation of that very important field, a recognition that too long has been lacking. He stated that we as a country will not progress in this century or the next until we give research the kind of attention it justly deserves.
I want to take a few minutes to dwell on this bill. I do so for several reasons. First, it has been a field of continuing interest to me. It is of continuing interest to the area I represent, both with regard to health research and medical research as well as the broader sense of industrial research. It is an area that is of great concern to me as an individual Canadian who believes that the future of this country is based on a recognition of research and what it can do for us.
It is somewhat ironic that this bill dealing with the elimination of the health resources fund should come up for debate in this House at the very time that a federal-provincial conference is being held just across the street from the Parliament Buildings. While the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the premiers meet to discuss federal-provincial co-operation on economic and fiscal matters, we are here discussing a bill that represents just one more example of the heavy-handed and unilateral approach of the federal government in its dealings with the provinces.

The irony is really just on the surface, since in all of the recent meetings between the federal and provincial first ministers the themes of federal interference in provincial affairs and provincial repercussions from federal action such as cutbacks in social programs emerge again and again. This is so because the government's commitment to consultation and co-operation is really very superficial, one to be dusted off and shown for display over national television when it pleases the government to do so, but quickly forgotten in the weeks and months that intervene. Certainly it is forgotten when it comes to policy formation and the impact of policy formation on the regions of this country. How else can we view the actions of the government when we are faced with such a blatant example of non-consultation as the demise, in this particular example, of the health resources fund?
Some provinces were indeed informed of the impending cutback, but none were consulted. For example, the minister of health in Manitoba was informed by telex five days after the announcement in the press. Some provinces were placed in the position where projects were already under way, projects they had been led to believe would be supported by ongoing funding from the health resources fund. True, the specific funds had not been committed, but the over-all budget was there. Now, according to the minister and the government, these funds will never be committed. The provinces will be asked, as they have been in many other cases, to pick up the tab.
This has been all too prevalent in some of the fiascos the government has introduced in recent months. For example, equalization cutbacks, a fund that is supposed to be a contract between 11 governments in this country. The equalization cutbacks were imposed unilaterally. Let the provinces shoulder the burden either by cutting back on essential programs or increasing taxes; that is the view of the federal government. Cutbacks to the unemployment insurance budget? Let the provinces make it up through welfare payments.
Here again with this bill we have the same attitude on the part of this government. The federal government says it will save $84 million, not by cutting back on its own operations, but by cutting back on provincial programs, and that without a word of prior consultation.
Not only does the cutback of the health resources fund represent another in a long series of blows to provincial budgets and provincial planning, but it is an indication of the irrationality of many of the cutbacks announced by the government since August. What is more, the government does not seem to recognize the irrationality and incohesion of many of the actions it has taken, it says in the name of restraint. It amazes me that government spokesmen seem to feel that their restraint program is a model of economic sense. Nothing they have done in the past ten years can be held up as a model of economic good sense.
Recently Treasury Board circulated a copy of a speech by the Comptroller General of Canada. It was a speech he had given to the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants on the problems and opportunities facing government as it accepts the challenge of fiscal restraint. I recommend it to members on
November 28, 1978

the government side. The speech was entitled "Controlling Federal Government Expenditures . . . Doing More with Less". What caught my eye was the title "Doing More with Less".
That is an admirable goal, one that could be easily attained by cutting waste and over-expenditure. The kind of overexpenditure referred to in the recent Senate report on accommodation would come under the category of doing more with less. That report showed that the government will be spending at least $179 million more in rent for office space over the next 35 years than if it had built the building itself.
Auditor Generals' reports are filled with examples of waste and over-expenditure that could be cut with no adverse effects on the taxpayers. The most recent report, the one we saw just last week, stated:
During the period of rapid expansion in the federal government it appears that the public purse was gradually deemed virtually bottomless.
The most recent report, the one we saw just last week, stated that during the period of rapid expansion in the federal government it appeared that the public purse was "gradually deemed virtually bottomless" and that there was very little attempt made to study whether or not a program was effective or efficient. It is both necessary and desirable to cut out waste and mismanagement in the spending of taxpayers' money. That is what I would call rational restraint-to cut out the fat and keep the meat; to do more with less. But some of the cuts which have been imposed during the government's burst of restraint are not that kind of restraint. They represent what I would call totally irrational restraint, restraint that does not make sense, restraint that keeps the fat and does away with the meat.
I received a letter earlier this year, in October, from the Canadian Federation of Biological Societies, a group of scientists very much concerned with the way the government is going in its irrational restraints upon scientific research. The letter reads:
While the recently announced federal cutbacks to health and education budgets do not as yet have operational meaning, they provide a clear indication of the government's current thinking and intentions. It is truly a hollow government policy that last June 1 proposes to stimulate research and development in this country and then, just a few months later, reneges on the same promises by cutting back on investment and innovation.
That letter, written before the introduction of this bill, reflects the concern which has been expressed by the biological scientists and by many others who are devoted to scientific and medical research. As they point out, restraint affecting research programs, restraint which is harmful in its effects, cannot be called rational. It is not "doing more with less." The long-term effect would be quite the opposite-doing less with more. This is because every dollar which is not spent on research today will mean about 20 additional dollars which will have to be spent tomorrow. That is not real restraint.
Some of the proposed cutbacks are likely to have very detrimental effects and their adverse impact on the economy is obvious. I could list a few. The termination of the health resources fund is a prime example, as are the cutbacks affect-
Health Resources Fund Act
ing the various branches of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
I think of the $3 million cut in the professional training program; the $4.8 million cut in the program concerning the non-medical use of drugs; the $2 million cutback in the national health research and development program, and the general reduction of $500,000 in the budget of the Medical Research Council.
Cuts of that kind are fairly obvious and we recognize immediately that they are capable of a serious adverse impact. But there are other cutbacks which are less obvious and whose potential for adverse impact is not so quickly discernible. I will list a few. There is the $1.3 million cutback in post-secondary education programs administered through the education, science and culture division of Industry, Trade and Commerce; there is the $1 million general reduction in the funds available to the National Research Council; there is the reduction of $300,000 in the budget of the Canada Council and of $2.1 million in the funding available to the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council. Nor does this list include the millions cut from research and development funding affecting agriculture, the environment and cultural programs.
All this makes one wonder what the government has against the whole field of scientific research. It does not have a good record anyway, as we all know. But at a time when we should be building the future of our country on scientific research and development, they are particularly hard to defend.
The minister makes light of these cutbacks. In an interview reported in the Ottawa Citizen on October 18 she said the cut of half a million dollars from the budget of the Medical Research Council was small in comparison with others, for example in comparison with the cut in the operations budget of her own department. She said it made only the smallest dent in the council's total budget for the support of research in 1978-79.
This ignores two things. First, it ignores the fact that there are many other cutbacks affecting medical research-I have already mentioned some of them-in addition to the cuts in the Medical Research Council's budget. It also ignores the fact that in terms of 1971-72 dollars the council's budget has decreased annually by an average of 7 per cent. So that represents a further reduction in an already inadequate medical research budget.
Furthermore, the cuts in the funding of the Medical Research Council, the national health research and development program and the professional training program will affect more than the researchers themselves. Their impact will go far beyond the immediate research community. The loss will affect the training of physicians and other health professionals and will directly reduce patient care as trained personnel leave Canada. That is one of the very real tragedies of the approach taken by the government to health care and research in general. It illustrates the lack of sensitivity and awareness in this field.

What we have as a result of severe spending cutbacks in a very important field is the Canadian research community's losing a number of its most brilliant people. Already the reality of the Canadian research situation has caused many scientists and technicians to abandon that particular livelihood here in Canada or, indeed, to go elsewhere to pursue it. This year, for example, of 23 new applications to the Medical Research Council for grants for programs which were analyzed and deemed worthy of support by the Medical Research Council, only three were funded. What happened to the other 20 researchers and their programs? What happened to the benefits they might have brought to this country?
The health resources fund which the minister is in the process of eliminating-and she has eliminated other programs in the social services field-has provided a means for continuing scientific development in all regions of this country. It has contributed to the expansion of university hospitals, research centres and medical library facilities as well as to general health and hospital services across this country. According to the minister's own figures which she quoted when she spoke in the debate the other day, the fund has increased the number of graduates in health manpower categories by up to 9,000 a year in the ten-year period between 1966 and 1976. In 1966 there were only nine graduate respiratory technologists in Canada. In 1976 there were 138. The number of graduate laboratory technologists in 1966 was 265. By 1977, thanks in part to this program, that number had risen to 1,200.
One might say that that is enough and that we should be content with that. That seems to be what the government is saying when it suggests cutting off this program and abandoning it before it has run its full course. "There are 1,200 graduate laboratory technologists; surely that should satisfy the Canadian market". That seems to be the way the government is approaching this, but that is part of the irrational thinking of this government when it comes to something like research and development in this country. We are a growing country. We are a developing country. We depend on research and technology to take us forward, but their funding and importance are being reduced by this government. The cutback about which I am talking will retard development and reduce the number of skilled and professional people in a field where they are much needed. The cutback will reduce their numbers as well as practical and theoretical medical facilities.
The health resources plan is a good plan. It has been working well. But in order to save $84 million over the next two and a half years the minister has served notice that she will be putting an end to any further commitments under the plan. The provinces are left holding the bag. There are planned and uncompleted projects. Not only that, Mr. Speaker, but, more importantly, Canadians in general are also being deprived of a program which would have benefitted each and every Canadian had it been allowed to continue.
In the light of so much waste in other areas, the government's allowing such a situation to develop is shameful. This cut is both unnecessary and irrational. Furthermore, in light of

the current tragic state of affairs in medical research generally and in light of cutbacks, hidden and otherwise, in other medical research funding, the termination of the health resources fund is just one more nail which the government seems willing to drive into the coffin of Canadian medical research. It is one more blow to the health scientists of this country and, regretfully, one more indication that the government does not recognize a dollar spent wisely. What is worse, it does not care.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker,

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to take part in this debate; however, faced with this despicable performance, quite unworthy of a serious member of this House, I cannot help but respond to the quite improper and quite unfair statements that have just been made by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander). Undoubtedly, the kind of remarks he just made before the House and the Canadian public listening through television will be judged according to their own merit by the Canadian public who has witnessed this shameful performance by the hon. member for Hamilton West, glass in hand, uttering quite improper and incongruous remarks.
What must be said about this proposal is that unfortunately, in these times of restraints, at a time when all Canadians urge the federal government and the provincial governments to reduce their expenditures as much as possible, so as to curb public spending, the Canadian government had to take some decisions and to make some budgetary cuts, obviously difficult to carry out but absolutely essential to maintain the Canadian economy.

I should like to say a few words in English, because the words expressed in the House were in English and they should be answered in the same language.
A policy of expenditure restraint had been advocated widely for some time. I am surprised to hear hon. members of the loyal opposition referring to a unilateral move by the federal government, when in fact there has been no such move. Such a policy of restraint is necessary to increase confidence in the Canadian economy, and to provide room for the private sector to expand and create jobs. Hon. members of the Conservative party have lost track of these important matters.
Expenditure restraint was a major feature of the federal anti-inflation program announced in the fall of 1975. In fact, this desire has been present since then. At the first ministers' conference last February, it was agreed that governments
November 28, 1978

should strive to reduce their rate of increase in expenditures to something less than the trend rate of growth of the gross national product. At their last conference, the ministers of finance agreed that restraint was necessary. It is with this high degree of consensus that the Canadian government implemented a substantial reduction of expenditures totalling $2.5 billion last summer.
I have heard members of the opposition expressing surprise and attempting to convey the message to the Canadian public that all of these matters were done unilaterally, without consulting the provinces. This is totally untrue and unfair.

I have been reading, as I am sure other members have, a book by William Simon of the United States entitled "A Time of Truth". I see the hon. member from Quebec city reading it.

I would refer hon. members to page 113 where Mr. Simon says some very enlightening things. He is speaking of those who have adopted the small "1" liberal ideology which he says:
-is actually committed to a steady erosion of our wealth and freedom, although its advocates are usually unaware of it.
They are unaware of it because they no longer know the relationship between wealth and freedom. Indeed, it is not too much to say that they no longer understand the concept of freedom. FDR actually redefined that concept, corrupting it so hopelessly that, save for a few philosophical diehards, succeeding generations were never again clear as to what it meant. Political freedom means only one thing: freedom from the state. FDR, however, invented a new kind of 'freedom': a government guarantee of economic security and prosperity. He thus equated "freedom" with cash. However desirable economic security may be-and it is profoundly desirable-it is not the same thing as political freedom.
He goes on a few sentences later to say:
The state ceased to be viewed as man's most dangerous enemy, to be shackled forever by constitutional chains. It was henceforth proclaimed to be the precise opposite; it became man's tenderhearted protector and provider. Statism and collectivism were brought into this country-by the back door-and, ironically, were heralded thereafter as the saving of free enterprise.
That is the significant change that has taken place in our countries, and I say that advisedly because it is a change that has taken place not only in this country and in the United States, but in England and many western democracies. There has been a change in philosophy. At one time we devoted all our energies to protecting ourselves from the state, or from intrusions by the state into our privacy and decision-making process. Now things have shifted to the point where we see the state as the power benefactor. One thing which the state does very well is govern, because it is designed to do that. It is infatuated with that process, and given the latitude and opportunity the state will govern. As readily as we are willing to turn over to the state the decision-making processes of our lives, even more ready to accept it is the state, to come into our lives and to take them over.
November 28, 1978

As I reflected on what Mr. Simon said, I could not help but flip over the pages of history in my mind and to think of the process of democratization of our countries. In the United States the watershed occurred in 1787 and 1789, when they passed their bill of rights which said in substance that Congress snail be prohibited from invading the lives of the individual citizens of that country. A few years later the republic of France did the same thing. One hundred years previous to that England passed its bill of rights as a statute, not as part of the constitution-because we all know that England does not have a constitution. When William and Mary took over the throne of England the good citizens had the foresight to ask for a bill of rights to ensure that the constitutional monarchy could not invade their private lives. That is the history of the democratization of the constitutions as we know them. Essentially they free us from arbitrary control by the state or the government.
Here we have a government that again moves into the area of arbitrary decision-making. A few years ago it instituted a program of training for health facilities in the provinces. It induces the provinces and twists their arms to participate in that process and to use their funds in it. Once their tax structure training facilities and their capital expenditures are committed, then all of a sudden the federal government says, "Too bad, we can't afford it any longer; you're on your own". These are the ways in which the federal government intrudes in our lives. They come to us as though they are the great benefactor of the citizens, but in actual fact they become our governors and our masters.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. Kenneth Robinson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: HEALTH AND WELFARE-REQUEST GOVERNMENT RECONSIDER CUT IN FAMILY PLANNING GRANTS PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Philbrook) on bringing the important matter of family planning before the House of Commons once again. The matter needs to be considered. I think all hon. members would agree that family planning is something about which we must be more concerned because of the tremendous population growth today.
Further to the question raised by the hon. member for Halton on November 17, I would like to add the following comments. The reduction in family planning grants for 19791980 is firm. The minister has no intention to review the cutbacks already announced since these reductions were based on very careful consideration of all the options available.
The minister does, of course, recognize the importance of prevention and the concern of the hon. member for the continuation of family planning services. I would like to remind the hon. member that these services are a provincial responsibility and that the Department of National Health and Welfare, through its special grants, has ensured that services are available for the residents of each province and territory.
In addition, welfare services are to be shared under the Canada Assistance Plan when provided by provincially-approved agencies-which are listed in an agreement under the Canada Assistance Plan-either to persons in need or to persons who are likely to become in need if they do not receive the services they require. Likelihood of need is determined on the basis of economic as well as social need criteria.
With regard to family planning services, certain services such as information, referrals and counselling have been accepted as welfare services for cost-sharing purposes under the Canada Assistance Plan. The essential point relative to cost sharing in welfare services is that federal contributions are made toward agency costs associated with the provision of such services.
The cost associated with providing family planning means- for example, the pill or IUDS-are cost-shared through the assistance provision of the Canada Assistance Plan when provided as items of assistance to persons in need.
In summary, 1 would like to assure the hon. member that the social services and health systems of the provinces will continue to receive the necessary funding to provide family planning services on a preventive basis to those in need.

URBAN AFFAIRS-INTERDEPARTMENTAL COMMITTEE TO STUDY URBAN AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to respond tonight to an answer given to me by the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) on November 15 when I questioned him in the House concerning the senior interdepartmental committee on urban affairs. I have with me tonight a copy of a report dated September, 1975. I asked the minister why this committee of deputy ministers has not met since 1975. It is important that this committee meet because when the Minister of State for Urban Affairs was first conceived, it was to be a co-ordinating ministry. The minister's function was to be only that which would co-ordinate activities related to housing and would include the co-ordination of programs affecting some ten other ministries. That was the promise given to the House of Commons when, some eight years ago, the government created the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs.
1 have here a confidential cabinet document dated July 3, 1973 when the cabinet discussed the need for this co-ordinating committee of deputy heads to discharge the mandate given to them by parliament which requires a high and continuing degree of interdepartmental consultation at the senior level-I am reading from this document. I also have another confidential cabinet document dated July 17, 1973, just a couple of weeks later. According to this document, the cabinet decided that it was critically important, in order to make the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs work effectively as a co-ordinating ministry, that there be established a senior interdepartmental committee on urban affairs to be composed of deputy heads. These were not just joe-boys or boys from the mail room; these were deputy ministers.
That is how important this committee was. Some of the responsibilities of that committee were to meet no less than twice a year at the call of the chairman; that is the deputy minister of state for urban affairs. Now that deputy head is Bill Teron. It was to assist in the preparation of, and to present to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs, the transmittal to cabinet of an annual review and evaluation of the range of federal programs which have significantly affected the urbanization of Canada. To this date we have had only one such report.
I maintain, sir, that one of the reasons this government is following the suggestion of the official opposition that the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs should be wound down is, that they failed to have the departmental heads meet as they were supposed to. You cannot have a ministry whose job it is to co-ordinate and report to the House of Commons through the minister not knowing whether or not they are doing the job of co-ordination. The only way to evaluate the efficiency of the ministry and of the programs that ministry was co-ordinating was to have an evaluation; but the people who were to do that job, the deputy heads, did not meet. So there was confusion and mismanagement. As a result the government decided, because the ministry has not been working, to disband it.

I commend the government for that decision because it is exactly what we on this side suggested a year and a half ago, namely, that the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs be dismantled because it has not been effective in co-ordinating the various programs. But the difference between what they are doing and what we would have done is simple. The government announced out of the blue this great revelation, this great turnabout last Friday, and not a province in the country knew it. No one knew it except the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the minister involved. It is that kind of mentality that has characterized this government-on-again-off-again, without consultation with the provinces.
On page 31 of the report of the western premiers task force on constitutional trends of last May, it is stated that in the broad area of housing consultation has been virtually nonexistent. They disband a whole ministry dealing with the whole range of programs in which the federal government involved the provinces, without even asking the provinces what they thought of the dismantling of the entire Ministry of State for Urban Affairs. It is that kind of irresponsible reflex action by the government that has put it into the position it enjoys today with the Canadian public. Now the Canadian public is determined to get rid of the government.
I applaud the government for innovative programs such as CHIP, NIP, RRAP and AHOP. If the government survived another couple of years, we would have had jump, skip and a lot of others. No program is meaningful unless it is evaluated. The government should take a second look at its programs to see whether they work, and if it was a targeted program, whether it had the effectiveness on the target area for which it was conceived. The government did not do that. It brought in a program of graduated payment mortgages, not knowing whether AHOP worked. There were massive defaults in AHOP. A senior departmental group was supposed to meet and evaluate these programs, and now the government is graduating payment mortgages. Right in the middle of all the new changes, the government said, "Sorry, boys, we are going to dismantle the ministry.'' That is an irresponsible government. Given the opportunity, at the drop of a writ we will replace them.

The senior interdepartmental committee on urban affairs was formed in 1973 to assist in the preparation of an annual review and evaluation of the range of federal programs which significantly affect the urbanization of Canada. Also it was to assist the Department of Urban Affairs in advising the Treasury Board secretariat and the Privy Council office on policy and program proposals of federal departments and agencies which could have a significant impact on urbanization and urban development patterns.

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: URBAN AFFAIRS-INTERDEPARTMENTAL COMMITTEE TO STUDY URBAN AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my comments tonight refer to the fact that the Canadian Wheat Board has put out tenders to purchase 500 to 2,000 hopper cars. I maintain that the Wheat Board was blackmailed into doing that by the fact that the railways of this country are on strike when it comes to purchasing more hopper cars. In other words, they are not doing it. The minister in charge of the Wheat Board has his hands tied by restraint and, therefore, he is not doing it either.
For the first time ever the producers, namely, the farmers of western Canada, are in the position where they, through their wheat boards, have to purchase between 500 and 2,000 hopper cars. I maintain that is a very, very dangerous precedent, a precedent that is being set which may end up being carried on.
Adjournment Debate
I think it is wrong. What other commodity group has to purchase the cars to move their goods? Do General Motors have to do it? Do big companies have to do it? Do the fishermen have to do this, or do other people have to do it? I maintain that in most cases the answer is no. Therefore, it is very dangerous to ask farmers to do it.
I want to give a few background facts showing why we are in this type of situation today, why the railroads have been blackmailing the Wheat Board, and why the government has been implicit in this action. First of all, the capacity to move grain in this country has been slipping drastically. In 1972 we had 22,000 boxcars. By July 31, 1978 we were down to 12,800 boxcars. In the meantime, the federal government had purchased some 8,000 hopper cars. One hopper car equals about 1.5 boxcars in terms of grain moving capacity. Therefore, if you add in the 8,000 hopper cars in terms of capacity to the 12,800 boxcars, our capacity would equal about 24,800 boxcars. Therefore, even though the government has purchased 8,000 hopper cars, we still had less grain moving capacity than we had in 1972 before that purchase. As a matter of fact, the system has a two-million bushel less carrying capacity today than it did in 1972.
To make matters worse, we need more hopper cars and grain cars for the future. The Wheat Board says we need 9,000 more cars. The Wheat Board breaks it down this way: We need 4,000 more hopper cars and we need to repair some 5,000 boxcars.
Forest Hetland, who is a commissioner of the Canadian Wheat Board, said that by 1985 Canada could be exporting about 20 million tonnes of wheat and ten million tonnes of feed grains. He said that 4,000 new hopper cars could generate over $700 million each year in increased export sales and foreign exchange earnings. Mr. Hetland went on to say that even at a cost of $50,000 each, or $200 million total, for these hopper cars this would still be a good long-term investment for Canada.
Charlie Gibbings, another commissioner of the Wheat Board, was quoted by the Leader Post as saying that car supply is the most immediate problem. He said that 20,000 hopper cars and 5,000 boxcars will be needed to meet the 1985 target of moving 30 million tonnes of grain.
Then we have Commissioner Kristjanson, assistant chief commissioner of the Canadian Wheat Board, a 19-year veteran with the Wheat Board, 13 years as a commissioner and therefore a man who knows a great deal about the business, who is confident that the board could achieve export sales of 30 million tonnes by 1985, which is a 50 per cent increase, if transportation systems improved. We need three essential ingredients, he suggested. We need a fleet of 20,000 grain hopper cars, a 20,000-tonne terminal facility at Prince Rupert and an improved system of rail delivery through the Rockies to the west coast. It is obvious we need more than a faster turnaround time, although we need that too. We need some 20,000 hopper cars and 5,000 boxcars to meet our target for 1985.

November 28, 1978
Adjournment Debate
What I am saying to the government now is that we need these hopper cars and we need them very fast. The fact that we do not have them now means we have lost sales. Our current inability to deliver has cost the Canadian farmers about $350 million in lost sales this year. Farmers have also lost about $25 million in demurrage charges this year because of the backlog, due to hopper cars and boxcars not being available. Last year, according to the advisory committee to the Canadian Wheat Board, transportation delays cost the Canadian farmer about $150 million.
Then we have the China sale. We sold around three million tonnes of grain to China this year. The Wheat Board tells me we could have sold around four million tonnes if we had had the proper facilities to move the grain. If we were really doing things well we could have sold about six million tonnes, as that is the amount of grain the Chinese wanted to buy. As it is, Canada sold about 21 million tonnes of grain in the last crop year. We could do a lot better. The main problem is that the railways are not providing the service they should to western farmers.
I am sure that the parliamentary secretary is very embarrassed about the government handouts to railways. The branch line subsidy to the railways by this government last year was $90 million, and the savings to the railway on the cost of capital and depreciation for government hopper cars, which are supplied by the government, was $35.7 million. The saving to the railway on the cost of capital and depreciation for branch line rehabilitation was $98 million, and on the cost of capital and depreciation on Canadian Wheat Board hopper cars $14 million. This amounts to a subsidy from this Santa Claus government of $237.7 million per year. At the same time the railway profits for the first nine months of 1978 were $163 million. In the new budget they will be getting another tax subsidy of 7 per cent for an investment tax credit on transportation equipment.
If we look at the subsidies the railways have received from this government and the profits they have made, there is no reason why they should not be supplying the hopper cars and repairing the boxcars, or that the farmers of western Canada or the Wheat Board area farmers should be purchasing between 500 and 2,000 hopper cars out of their own money. It is a dangerous precedent that should not be allowed to happen. The government has an obligation to force the railways to purchase those cars, and if it cannot force the railways, then it has the obligation to provide the cars itself.

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles Lapointe (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: URBAN AFFAIRS-INTERDEPARTMENTAL COMMITTEE TO STUDY URBAN AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is worth remembering that over the last five years the government has added 8,000 hopper cars to the grain transportation network at an approximate cost of $260 million. It is also worth mentioning that during the past two years an amount of $170 million has been invested to improve railways in the prairie provinces and that

the government is committed to earmark another $500 million in the next five or seven years to complete the upgrading of railways throughout western Canada.
When the railway companies tell us that they have enough hopper cars and boxcars for the transportation of grain, it is then a matter of interpretation and also a very complex issue. The minister stated today that he does not quite agree with the Canadian Pacific for instance which is of the opinion that the required number of cars is presently in use throughout the Canadian Pacific network. The minister has even offered a new arrangement to this company and to the Canadian National for the joint financing of a car repair program.
As I stated earlier, Mr. Speaker, this issue concerning the number of cars which might be needed is further complicated by the fact that it boils down to the question of knowing how many round trips are made by the cars between the prairies and Thunder Bay on the one side and the west coast on the other side. One also has to know if we have the minimum number of cars required to satisfy regular needs or if we have at our disposal the required number which would meet the requirements of a peak season when necessary, even if it is only a matter of five or six weeks during the grain shipment period.
The railway companies have suggested that the required number of cars is available, yet it remains rather difficult to determine in advance how many cars will be needed.
The Canadian Wheat Board and the minister, as he stated himself this afternoon, are convinced that more cars will be needed in a rather near future. The Canadian Wheat Board may differ with the railway companies in its interpretation of what constitutes a sufficient number of cars. The board must be concerned about the fact that it could have to pay demurrage charges. Consequently, the cars that the board would purchase would enable it to avoid paying demurrage charges during future peak periods on the market. For their part, the producers share the concerns of the board and, through their representatives on the Canadian Wheat Board, they accepted in principle this purchase proposal when the board consulted them. I also want to mention or emphasize the other initiatives taken by the minister in this regard. Since the branch line rehabilitation program is now being implemented, cars presently available and those that the board could acquire later on will be put to a better and more effective use.
As for ensuring a better use of the whole system, the minister reminded the House this afternoon during oral question period that he has appointed an analyst to study grain handling and transport operations and to make suggestions to improve these operations. The very recent up-date of the Snavely report, which was published a while ago, shows that major improvements have already been made as concerns the use of railway cars. Nevertheless, we must determine whether it is possible to do more and to make other improvements in the near future.
November 28, 1978
